extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, journalism students, and media professionals thinking about technology's impact on news
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and adapting news-gathering, editing, and distribution practices in the face of new technologies (citizen contributions, tagging, RSS, algorithmic selection). Focus is on how technology changes tasks traditionally done by journalists and how to preserve core journalistic values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Being Native American meant he could not be objective in his reporting (an editor's view); reporters have an obligation to fairness and the skills to live up to this responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The anecdote about Tim Giago highlights that newsroom decisions about who can report on certain beats implicate perceptions of objectivity. Evaluate whether coverage practices allow fair representation and whether journalists are trained and supported to meet obligations of fairness rather than being excluded for identity-based assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Napsterization (disintermediation) vs. algorithm journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Tension between the “napsterization of news” (everybody communicates and contributes) and “algorithm journalism” (computers executing tasks traditionally reserved for journalists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess where a given practice lies on the spectrum from disintermediation/democratization to automated algorithmic control. Consider benefits of broader participation (citizen voices) alongside risks of outsourcing editorial judgment to software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of technology to augment vs. substitute human judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The situation follows a pattern between those who wanted computers to substitute for human tasks and those who wanted them used to augment capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a technological tool is being used to support journalists (augment) or to replace essential human judgment (substitute). Prefer workflows where technology increases reporters' capacity without eliminating verification, context, and editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen journalism contributions and credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: People who have not received any journalism training contribute to news coverage by supplying stories and commentary with words or images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When incorporating citizen contributions, evaluate credibility, verification processes, and the value added (local perspective, immediacy) versus potential misinformation. Institutions should develop standards for accepting, verifying, and labeling user-generated content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mobile devices and accessible multimedia tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices (e.g., Nokia phones with cameras/editing) let people shoot video, edit with music, and send it to blogs, wikis, or news sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure submissions and reporting workflows by ease of capture, basic editorial quality (composition, audio clarity), and the ability to integrate multimedia into storytelling. Encourage training on basic production and ethical standards for contributors using such devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folksonomy and user tagging as editorial categorization
rubrics_metrics.description: At del.icio.us and sites like Flickr and Technorati users can tag pages/photos—'folksonomy'—which helps categorize news and can do what editors usually do, while also commenting on the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tagging systems for usefulness in discovery and categorization, their susceptibility to noise or manipulation, and how they complement or conflict with professional metadata/editorial taxonomies. Use them to augment editorial discovery while maintaining quality controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalized aggregation (RSS) and user selection of feeds
rubrics_metrics.description: RSS feeds allow users to select and collect bits of information from different media, using programs or web pages where chosen feeds are constantly updated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider personalization as a distribution criterion: evaluate the balance between user control over consumed content and the role of editors to surface important but less-personalized stories. Provide clear signals about source credibility in aggregated feeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic reorganization of site content and story importance
rubrics_metrics.description: News changes fast so a paper’s web site is constantly reorganized by algorithms that determine image position and story importance as it unfolds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize algorithmic ranking for biases, responsiveness to breaking events, and transparency. Decide which decisions require human editorial intervention (e.g., sensitive images, controversial framing) and which can be safely automated for speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated aggregation without human intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Google News and similar services rely on computers to collect and distribute emerging stories without human intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using or designing fully automated aggregators, evaluate their source-selection criteria, error rates, and propensity to amplify false or unverified information. Implement oversight or correction mechanisms where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-detection automation and user-directed feeds
rubrics_metrics.description: Envisioned systems where cameras and software detect events (e.g., 'an accident') and send images to users who preselected interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess automation by its detection accuracy, privacy and ethical implications (surveillance concerns), and relevance matching to user preferences. Include opt-in controls and human review for potentially sensitive or legally fraught content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of information volume and speed on journalistic methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Volume and speed of information now being collected and distributed contribute to use of technology to execute tasks previously done by journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate methods for coping with scale: selective aggregation, automated triage, and prioritization policies. Ensure speed does not completely override verification and contextual reporting standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratization and audience authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Napsterization may be understood as a democratization of journalism; young people want to assume authorship of the narratives of their own lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value audience participation and decentralization as positive, but measure how to integrate audience authorship while maintaining editorial standards and public-interest reporting. Engage communities while preserving investigative capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving essential journalistic values while adapting
rubrics_metrics.description: The challenge for journalists resides in how to best adapt while preserving the essential values of our craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a high-level criterion: any technological or organizational change should be evaluated against core journalistic values (fairness, accuracy, verification, accountability, public-interest focus). Resist changes that sacrifice these values for novelty or speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to younger audiences and narrative expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Young people disbelieve in metanarratives and want their voices heard; they have instant access to information and know local contexts better than many journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure journalistic work for its resonance with younger audiences: provide avenues for participation, adapt storytelling formats to decentralized authorship, and prioritize topics that matter to these audiences without abandoning journalistic rigor.
